newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand discussing economic revival with IMF.
newsitem.headline: Thailand discussing economic revival with IMF.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said on Monday that he was meeting five IMF officials this week in Bangkok to seek their advice on ways to revive the country's battered economy.
"We have been working actively with the IMF and we should be able to wrap it up within one week," he told reporters.
He added that Thai economic ministers would on Monday discuss a rescue package for the flagging economy that would not cover the question of borrowing from the world body.
The rehabilitation package drawn up by Thanong needs the endorsement of the economic ministers before going to the cabinet for final approval.
"The package will involve finding systematic measures to shore up the economy," Thanong said.
"We have been in consultation with the IMF for the past month," he added.
On the meeting with the IMF team, Thanong said he expected to wrap it all up within one week. "I expect it will go smoothly," he added.
On the possibility of Thailand borrowing from the IMF, Thanong said that the issue was on hold until after the rescue package was approved by the cabinet.
"At this time, we need to set the priorities on how to tackle problems and set our targets. Once confidence of investors is restored funds will flow back automatically (to Thailand)," he said.
Thanong said his economic rehabilitation package would include fiscal and monetary measures as well as deal with the question of the level at which the embattled baht should stand.
"We feel that it is too cheap," he said when asked about the baht which has been trading since late last week at around the 32 baht level, after briefly hitting a new record low of 32.70.

Thailand is going through its worst economic slump in more than a decade with the growth set to slow to around four percent. Its financial and property sectors have been hard hit by tight liquidity and non-performing loans.

The nation's economic woes have prompted economists and analysts to urge the government to seek IMF financial assistance to regain lost investor confidence in the country. But Thailand initially said it was not seeking IMF assistance.
Analysts have estimated that Thailand would need about $10-20 billion to help it overcome financial problems.
High interest rates have choked domestic business activity and doubts over Thailand's economic soundness have prompted foreign banks to slow their lending to Thai corporates.
"We fully appreciate the frustration faced by businessmen because of the drying up of foreign loans and liquidity. They have our sympathy," Thanong said.
"As we have seen, spotty unsystematic measures cannot restore confidence. If we adopt comprehensive measures it can help restore currency stability more quickly," he added.

"The current liquidity problem can be compared to a leaking barrel. No matter how much we fill it in, it keeps leaking out. But if we plug the holes, it can stop the leak and liquidity can be refilled easily," he said.
